newsitem.title: USA: Nicaraguans have mixed reaction to Reno decision.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguans have mixed reaction to Reno decision.

text.p: Nicaraguan immigrants on Friday lauded Attorney General Janet Reno's initiatives to prevent mass deportations and help some immigrants stay in the United States, but said the reforms did not go far enough.
In a symbolic gesture, one Nicaraguan immigrant in Miami ended a 36-day hunger strike to thank Reno and another began a fast to demand permanent resident status.

"Some part of our community now has a solution, maybe 5,000 people. This is a good first step," Luis Vanega, director of the Nicaraguan Patriotic Union, told a news conference. "But we want a solution for all our people."

Reno on Thursday unveiled a plan to review and likely suspend a ruling by the Immigration Appeals Board that could have resulted in mass expulsions, and to send legislation to Congress to ease restrictions on immigrants.

The board ruling had left hundreds of thousands of immigrants from Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala and other countries open to deportation, even though they had earlier qualified to remain in the United States.

Angrily, they filed a class action lawsuit against the government, and last month won a U.S. judge's permission to stay at least until a hearing next year. Leaders of several Central American countries also had pleaded with President Bill Clinton to prevent deportations, fearing damage to their economies if the immigrants were returned en masse.

Jose de Carmen Garay-Vanegas, 27, who said he fought with the Contra army in Nicaragua when he was 14 and had been in the United States more than ten years, said Reno's initiatives would ease the pain of Nicaraguans who felt their rights had been trampled.

"She is conscious that they took away the rights of the people who had been here for years," he said. "I would like to thank her for the Nicaraguan people. Now they have the right to go to court again to have a solution."
But some advocates were more cautious, vowing to continue their political fight until the U.S. granted resident status.
"We are hoping for good news from the Congress and President Clinton by the end of the year," said Nesto Nunez, president of the United Organisation of Nicaraguan Exiles.

Mario Palma, who began a hunger strike 36 days ago, said he was ending his fast because of Reno's decision. "The decision is not complete, but it is something to solve the problems of Nicaraguans," he said.
But Isidro Bonilla, another member of the Miami immigrant community, said he was beginning a hunger strike "because we don't have permanent status."

Miami immigration lawyer Ira Kurzban, who filed the suit on behalf of those affected by the immigration board ruling, praised Reno's decision but said it did not resolve the issue of a cap of 4,000 people per year who qualify for residency.
